doc.title: Arthur Baron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Deaths and the state of the country
title: Losing Bucky Pizzarelli and playing with 102-year-old Fred Staton
summary: Baron remembers Bucky Pizzarelli and nursing-home gigs with Fred Staton, who played at 102.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yes. There was a week, shortly after your last gig, where it seemed like every other day some well known, much loved musicians were showing up in the obit section.
I’m wondering if you were close to any of them.

A lot of them. Bucky Pizzarelli. Bucky had a lot of, a lot of friends. I’m not claiming sole ownership, you know, and I didn’t see him that much, but as he got older, I met him in a recording session a zillion years ago and he always remembered me. Months could go by and I started — for a while there was this organization at Lincoln Center, not even actually part of Jazz at Lincoln Center, it was PTSPD — not the post traumatic syndrome but similar letters. And they got a lot of nursing home gigs and things like that. And I had great players. I don’t know if you remember Fred Staton, you met Fred of course, you know Fred. You knew him. He was in his late 90s when we were doing these gigs. And you know he did — the last gig he did I believe was with my band at an open air church gig down here at St. Mark’s Church. He was 102 and he was playing his arse off. And at the end of the gig I said, “Fred, did you have a good time?” He said, “Man, I couldn’t find a reed the whole gig.” 102. I said — that was just cracked me up. And I looked at him and I said, “Fred, you’re still doing it.”
Whatever you got give me some.
